GIC, one of Anthropic’s largest investors, to stay invested beyond IPO

FAST

SINGAPORE: GIC intends to stay invested in Anthropic beyond its initial public offering (IPO) , with its partnership with the Claude developer already extending beyond capital. Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund is now one of Anthropic’s largest investors, having participated in three funding rounds in less than a year, said Chris Emanuel, head of GIC’s Technology Investment Group in a LinkedIn post on Friday (Nov 20). “An IPO is an important milestone, but it’s just one moment in a company’s journey,” he said. “We invest across multiple rounds, through the IPO and beyond. That’s lifecycle investing in practice.”

Mr Emanuel’s remarks follow the artificial intelligence company’s record-breaking Wall Street debut on Thursday. Anthropic, the first major frontier AI model developer to go public, clinched the largest stock market debut on record, raising about US$81.3 billion and valuing the company at about US$1.5 trillion on a fully diluted basis. The company priced its shares at US$83 apiece, above its previously targeted range of US$70 to US$78, after increasing the size of its offering to 980 million shares amid strong investor demand. Anthropic’s shares rose as much as 39 per cent to US$115.10 before paring gains to close at US$97.17, 17 per cent above the IPO price, and giving the company a valuation of just below US$1.8 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

Related:

Anthropic clinches biggest IPO ever with US$81 billion offering

Anthropic pulled off the biggest IPO ever. What that means, by the numbers

PARTNERSHIP BEYOND CAPITAL  Mr Emanuel said GIC’s partnership with Anthropic has grown “well beyond the check”, with the sovereign wealth fund drawing on its broader platform to help meet the company’s AI infrastructure needs, connect it with senior business leaders and support its international expansion. He described the investment as an example of “lifecycle investing” – backing companies across different stages and drawing on the fund’s broader capabilities to support them. The sovereign wealth fund has also invested in Ode, an AI services company that helps enterprises implement Anthropic’s technology. Bloomberg reported that the fund has invested more than US$4.5 billion in Anthropic across its last three funding rounds. GIC’s stake in Anthropic was worth about US$15 billion at the IPO price, according to Bloomberg estimates. The first of those investments came in Anthropic’s US$13 billion Series F funding round in September 2025, which valued the company at US$183 billion. GIC and US investment firm Coatue then led Anthropic’s US$30 billion Series G funding round in February, which valued the company at US$380 billion. The fund was also among the co-leads of Anthropic’s US$65 billion Series H round in May, which valued the company at US$965 billion. Mr Emanuel said the partnership with Anthropic began even before the first investment. He added that Anthropic stood out during the fund’s research into the frontier model market. The company’s technical capabilities, mission and commitment to developing frontier AI safely and responsibly further strengthened GIC’s conviction, he said.

Warm embrace, fragile truce: Trump-Xi goodwill faces fresh tests after APEC summit

Fresh US curbs on AI chips, an unfinished tariff deal and shifting political dynamics in Washington threaten to test the limit of the fragile US-China detente, analysts say.

FAST

SHENZHEN: Since taking office in 2013, Chinese President Xi Jinping had never personally welcomed another leader at the airport. But this week, he did. When Air Force One touched down in Shenzhen on Wednesday (Nov 18), Xi was waiting on the red carpet for United States President Donald Trump. The two men embraced briefly before walking to their waiting cars - past performers cheering and waving pom-poms. It was a favour returned. Months earlier in September, Trump greeted Xi on arrival at Joint Base Andrews, a US military airfield outside Washington.

The exchange set the tone for the pair’s third meeting this year, held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

Chinese President Xi welcomes Donald Trump as he arrives at Shenzhen Airport on Nov 18, 2026. REUTERS/Carlos Barria

Xi spoke of the “overall stability and positive momentum” in ties, according to an official Chinese readout. Trump hailed a “very special relationship”. But while courtesies are being returned, fresh US curbs on artificial intelligence (AI) chips and an undelivered tariff deal threaten to test that spirit of reciprocity. Beijing is prepared to answer further US restrictions in kind, analysts told CNA - raising questions over how long a fragile detente can hold.

Related:

China slams new US chip curbs, vows 'necessary measures'

Chinese tech firms fear AI hits from US curbs after Nvidia fallout

RECIPROCITY ON DISPLAY Xi's airport reception is very much “just a reciprocal move”, said Guo Shan, a research economist and partner at Hutong Research. Trump “desperately needed a win” after midterm losses and Xi gave him a stage, said James Chen, assistant professor of diplomacy and international relations at Tamkang University in Taipei. “Xi extended Trump a warm welcome and lavish hospitality, while Trump elevated Xi's international stature to unprecedented heights,” Chen told CNA. Back in September, both leaders agreed that ties should rest on “respect, fairness and reciprocity”, according to Chinese readouts. On Thursday, they agreed to draw up “an action plan on building a constructive relationship of strategic stability”, China's readout of the meeting said. The guiding role of head-of-state diplomacy is “irreplaceable”, Xi told Trump in comments carried by Chinese state media outlets.

Trump pats Xi's back at the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen. (Photo: CNA/Tan Wen Lin)

The line was aimed at Washington, said William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at International Crisis Group. It was Beijing “trying to preach to the US and the wider American foreign policy circle” about the dividends of the past year, Yang said. Without the two sides talking, the tariff truce struck in October 2025 would not have been extended to Jan 10, 2027, Guo said. “I think as long as you and I are in charge of things, we’ll never have a problem,” Trump told Xi. Some analysts are less sure - starting with how far Trump is still in charge. Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the Nov 3 midterm elections.

Related:

US midterms: Democrats' victory puts Trump's China diplomacy to the test

Tensions rise as midterm campaign ends with control of Congress at stake

“The room for Trump to deliver whatever he promised has declined after the midterms,” said Guo. Chim Lee, senior analyst at Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU), said Beijing still sees the US president as a check on harder-line voices in Washington. “China also sees that Trump can be a stabilising factor within all of the different risk factors that can emerge in the US," Lee said.  CHIP CURBS, COMPETING VISIONS FOR GOVERNANCE AI chips were among the most closely watched issues going into the meeting - but did not come up in Trump’s opening remarks to Xi or in China’s readout. The White House has yet to release its own. Trump did speak about chips elsewhere. In an interview with Fox News this week, he suggested that the US could allow sales of Nvidia's Blackwell chips to China in two or three years - once they are no longer the most advanced.

The NVIDIA logo on the exterior of NVIDIA's Shanghai office building in Shanghai. (Photo: REUTERS/Go Nakamura)

On Monday, the US Commerce Department tightened export controls to stop Chinese firms from tapping advanced American AI chips through data centres in third countries. The rule, which took effect on Thursday, requires licences for shipments of such chips to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil, with an exemption for US-headquartered companies. Beijing bristled. China’s commerce ministry said on Tuesday that it was strongly dissatisfied, adding that countermeasures would be taken if Washington pressed ahead. On Thursday, Xi was quoted in official handouts as saying that differences which cannot be resolved for now “should be managed in a constructive way, and escalation should be prevented”. “Beijing has prepared for a worst-case scenario, but unless it is compelled to respond, it would prefer to keep a low profile and wait for Washington's next move,” said Tamkang University's Chen. On its end, Washington too has held back. Trump has put off tougher chip limits, according to US media reports. “I don't think you want to insult China just before you get there,” Trump told reporters on Monday, when asked about divisions in his administration over how hard to press Beijing.

Related:

US signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months, House committee says

Commentary: Jensen Huang’s downfall will accelerate US-China ‘great decoupling’

The curbs landed amid an open rift in Trump's Cabinet.  Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said last week he was frustrated by delays at the Commerce Department, led by Howard Lutnick, in restricting exports of certain Nvidia chips to China, the Associated Press reported. Chen said the dispute “appears less like a broader US-China confrontation and more like an internal power struggle” between the two camps. But Beijing’s patience also has its limits. EIU’s Lee pointed to the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware (MATCH) Act, a Bill introduced in the US Congress in April that would restrict sales of chipmaking equipment to China. “These are likely to be a pretty big red line for China, and China has made it very clear that if you touch on some of the major issues, (they) will be willing to retaliate,” Lee said.

Xi and Trump attend a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC Leaders' Summit on Nov 19, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Sputnik/Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool)

There is precedent. In September 2025, the US extended export restrictions to subsidiaries of blacklisted companies. China responded the next month with sweeping controls on rare earths. Both sides shelved the measures under the truce. Trump and Xi also struck different notes on governing AI. Trump told APEC leaders on Thursday that the US opposes “any form of globalist regulation” of AI. According to official Chinese readouts, Xi said the two countries should “ensure that AI is always under human control”. But Trump told Fox News that he and Xi both want moderate AI regulations for safety and would work together on them, Reuters reported. Washington proposed an AI “notification mechanism” in September, but Guo said the chance of talks on AI safety has probably narrowed since a scandal over Nvidia chips allegedly diverted to China. “China sees that there is an internal fight in the US and they don't really know who they can talk to,” she added.

Related:

‘Security makes prosperity possible’: Xi urges Asia-Pacific cooperation at APEC summit

World leaders are coming to Shenzhen. What is China’s APEC message?

RECIPROCITY PUT TO THE TEST Trump told Xi that each side had agreed to cut tariffs on US$30 billion of trade, under what he called the “30-for-30” deal. “We have split up the tariffs and done it in a very fair way,” Trump said. Then came the ask. “I'll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” Trump told Xi during the opening of their bilateral meeting on Thursday - to push Beijing to purchase more American agricultural products. Before the summit, US officials said China had yet to fully honour its pledges to buy more American farm goods, according to US media reports. China has already been buying more, noted Guo - but it still wants Washington to cut back on tariffs on Chinese consumer goods before it commits to further purchases. “Fair treatment has to be on both sides,” said Guo. The deal had yet to be finalised as of last week, according to Reuters. “If we cannot deliver even on this small amount of products, then how do we talk about the broader deal?” Guo said.

Related:

Proposed US-China ‘Board of Trade’ may steady ties but expectations diverge ahead of Trump-Xi summit

Commentary: In trade’s ‘law of the jungle’, the winners are clear

US and Chinese officials held the first meeting of their Board of Trade by video link on Nov 13, according to China’s commerce ministry.  The ministry said on Thursday that the board's agriculture working group would hold its first meeting soon. Yang from the International Crisis Group is “sceptical” about the amount of details and consensus reached at working level on the board’s rules. “Essentially the idea of this meeting is really just to say, 'Let's just keep talking, we are not trying to just flip the table',” said EIU’s Lee. Both leaders are soon expected to meet again in December - at the G20 Leaders’ Summit in Miami. But Yang is less optimistic about the outlook. Once the new Congress convenes in January, he expects a more “tit-for-tat, competitive dynamic” - with China falling back on restricting rare earth exports. “The window to really preserve this detente is closing,” he said.

Source: CNA/xy(ht)

FAST

TOKYO, Nov 20 : Japanese soccer official Kozo Tashima said on Friday that the handling of Folarin Balogun's red card at the World Cup was what prompted him to run for the role of FIFA president against Gianni Infantino. FIFA suspended forward Balogun's automatic one-match ban for a red card in July, allowing the American striker to play against Belgium after US President Donald Trump said he had personally asked President Infantino to review the sanction. The decision triggered a swift and fiery backlash and, along with an aborted attempt to sell a stake in FIFA tournaments, fuelled opposition to Infantino's reelection as president. Tashima said he wanted to restore trust in FIFA, drawing parallels with 2016, when Infantino took charge after a corruption scandal.

"Ten years ago something similar happened, and Mr. Infantino became president to reform and improve things," the Japan Football Association (JFA) honorary president told a press conference. "He has certainly done wonderful things. But in this year, 2026, ten years later, events have occurred that ignored governance.  "I have worked in soccer, especially as a player and coach. As such, I cannot accept Balogun's red card in any way. On top of that, no explanation has been given even now. I felt very indignant about this, and that is why I decided to stand here." Following the Balogun incident, FIFA's disciplinary committee said it had the authority to suspend the one-match ban, and that it operated independently. FIFA last month said it would amend the rule in its disciplinary code which allowed for the reversal of the ban. WORKING WITH DIALLO The election, set to be held in March next year, will be the first time since he won the post in 2016 that Infantino will face a challenge after being reelected unopposed in 2019 and 2023. French Football Federation President Philippe Diallo also announced a challenge on Monday with the backing of European governing body UEFA. Infantino has the support of Asia and Africa's confederations. "I have not actually received a nomination from any continental confederation. So I'm well aware that I'm at a considerable disadvantage in this race," Tashima said.  "It's a fact that Gianni's support has been gradually declining. I will keep appealing to voters." Diallo said at a press conference on Tuesday that he would reach out to Tashima to "unite forces". Tashima said he was open to the idea of coordinating with the Frenchman's team to avoid splitting the anti-Infantino vote.  "I don't think the French candidate's entry puts me at a disadvantage. In fact, France has ties to Africa and other regions, so Mr. Diallo's entry may bring those votes," he added.  "Watching his press conference, I saw that he pointed out FIFA's accounting and other figures in great detail. I find it reassuring that such a professional has joined." 'LEAST CONSPICUOUS' FIFA PRESIDENT Tashima is a former Japan international and youth coach and the first Japanese candidate to stand for FIFA president. He has served on the FIFA Council since 2015. The 68-year-old said that if elected, he would shun the spotlight. "A foreign media person described me very accurately," he said. "They said that if I'm elected, I might become the least conspicuous president ever," he said.  "That may have been a bit of irony, but I'm fine with it. It's not the president who should stand out, but the players." He added that he would need to be modest in his campaigning, much of which would be funded by his own money.  "The JFA's budget for this year is already set, so of course, I would like support from the JFA, but we'll also have to gather funds, for example by creating a fund or running crowdfunding," he said.  "I won't spend wastefully. I also have no intention of flying by private jet or anything like that."

Source: Reuters

LAS VEGAS, Nov 19 : Cadillac Formula One CEO Dan Towriss said the US-backed team was focused on building for the future after retaining Valtteri Bottas for 2027, a decision that ended Colton Herta's immediate hopes of becoming the first American race driver for the new entrant. Cadillac confirmed on Wednesday that 10-times Grand Prix winner Bottas would remain alongside Mexican Sergio Perez for the team's second Formula One season, despite speculation that IndyCar race winner Herta could replace the Finn. The decision leaves Herta, Cadillac's test driver, weighing options such as a reserve role with the team and opportunities outside Formula One, Towriss told reporters at the Las Vegas Grand Prix. "There are a number of options on the table for Colton," Towriss said. "We've offered a reserve position, the seat's open for 2028 ... there are other options in other sports as well."

TOUGH DISCUSSION The 26-year-old Californian moved to Formula Two with Hitech this year in pursuit of the super licence points needed to race in Formula One. Herta endured a difficult season in the junior category but had impressed Cadillac in Formula One practice and testing, Towriss said. "It was definitely a tough decision, a tough discussion with Colton," he added. "He was disappointed. There was a lot of work, a lot of build-up going to this." Cadillac, backed by General Motors and TWG Motorsports, are bottom of the 2026 constructors' standings with no points in their debut campaign. In the 2026 drivers' championship, Bottas sits 23rd and Perez sits 24th, both with zero points. VALUABLE EXPERIENCE  Towriss said the team had expected a difficult first season after designing a car without the benefit of previous track data and having little more than a year to prepare for competition against established rivals. "We knew that it was a tough battle," he said. "We had a car that was designed without any track data, and we're competing against the 10 best teams in the world that have been doing this for a long, long time." He said the experience gained in 2026 would be valuable as Cadillac prepares its 2027 car, with the team now able to draw on race data and lessons from its first full season. Cadillac also needed to develop organisationally after an "all hands on deck" effort to get its first car onto the grid, Towriss said. SALE SPECULATION Towriss declined to comment on reports that Mark Walter, CEO and co-chairman of TWG Global, was considering selling his stake in the team.  Since Walter's insurance firms have been under investigation, Walter has sold his majority stake in the Los Angeles Lakers in a reported $12.5 billion deal in August, his 13 per cent stake in Chelsea of the English Premier League, and is reportedly nearing a sale of the WNBA's Los Angeles Sparks.  Towriss said nothing was affecting Cadillac's operations or personnel. "Our focus is just on the performance of the team," he said.

Source: Reuters

TAMPA, Florida: A US judge in Florida on Thursday (Nov 19) declared Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Britain's Duchess of Sussex, Meghan Markle, to be mentally competent to answer to a federal court charge accusing him of being a child sexual predator. Accepting the findings of a court-appointed forensic psychiatrist, US Magistrate Judge Lindsay Griffin ruled the 82-year-old father-in-law of Prince Harry was mentally fit to understand the proceedings against him and to properly assist in his own defence, court records showed. Neither prosecutors nor the defence disputed the findings of the psychiatrist's evaluation, contained in a 15-page report and based in large part on the doctor's in-person interview with Markle in prison last week. Markle was charged on Nov 5 in a criminal complaint with a single felony count of possessing child sexual abuse images.

According to an FBI affidavit filed with the complaint, the material in question, including two explicit photos of Markle posed with a naked underage girl and other images of him with children in various stages of undress, was found in two Los Angeles storage units. Commenting on the case at the time of Markle's arrest on Nov 6 at an assisted-living centre in Florida, FBI Director Kash Patel said Markle had "targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions". Griffin's ruling capped a competency proceeding set in motion by the judge after Markle's first court hearing on the day of his arrest. In ordering a psychiatric examination of the defendant, Griffin wrote that she found "reasonable cause" to believe Markle was suffering from some mental deficiency, based in part on his advanced age and "lack of recall" during his first court appearance the day of his arrest. Dr Aime Gerodimos, who conducted the evaluation, wrote in her report that Markle appeared to suffer from a "major neurocognitive disorder," possibly the result of mild vascular disease. She also found he was likely "exaggerating deficits" when asked to recall specifics of the allegations against him. The psychiatrist concluded that Markle "does have sufficient present ability to understand the nature and consequences of the proceedings against him and to assist properly in his defence" - the legal standard for a criminal defendant to be deemed competent.

It remained unclear when Markle would be transferred to federal custody in California, where the case against him was lodged. The judge on Thursday set a preliminary hearing in the case for Dec 1 in Tampa. According to the FBI affidavit, federal agents acting on a search warrant earlier this month seized a large cache of slides, film negatives and books from two storage lockers Markle had rented in Los Angeles since 2008. One of the photos showed a naked girl in a room that appears to be part of a motel chain in the Philippines, where Markle previously resided and where authorities initiated an investigation of him last month, the affidavit said. Philippine police said on Wednesday criminal complaints had been filed against Markle in the country’s Cebu province, where he lived. The complaints accuse Markle of violating local laws against online sexual abuse and exploitation of children, police said. Markle has denied the allegations, telling the Daily Mail the claims were untrue and describing them as "sick lies." Meghan Markle, an American actor, has been estranged from her father since the run-up to her marriage to King Charles' younger son, Harry, in 2018, when the duchess has said she first became aware of the allegations against her father.
